1-1.text: Part one. Energy stores. ... Energy makes things happen. We measure energy in joules. The short way to write joules is J.

1-2.text: Energy is kept in stores. Food, fuels and batteries have energy in a chemical store.

1-3.text: Anything that is moving has energy in its kinetic store. The faster it goes, the more energy.

1-4.text: Anything lifted up high has energy in its gravitational store. The higher it is, the more energy.

1-5.text: Stretched or squashed things, like a rubber band or a spring, have energy in an elastic store.

1-6.text: Hot things have more energy in their thermal store than cold things. There are a few more stores too, like magnetic and nuclear.

2-1.text: Part two. Energy transfers. ... Energy can move from one store to another. This is called an energy transfer.

2-2.text: A ball falls off a shelf. It gets lower, so its gravitational store empties. It gets faster, so its kinetic store fills up.

2-3.text: Energy is transferred in four main ways: by a force (mechanically), electrically, by heating, and by light and sound.

2-4.text: A torch: the battery's chemical store is transferred electrically to the bulb. The bulb gives out light, and it also heats the surroundings a little.

3-1.text: Part three. Energy is never used up. ... Here is a very important rule: energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred.

3-2.text: An old filament light bulb is given 100 joules of energy electrically. 20 joules comes out as light. 80 joules heats the room.

3-3.text: 20 joules plus 80 joules equals 100 joules. All the energy is still there. None of it has vanished.

3-4.text: The light is the useful energy. The heating is wasted energy. Wasted energy spreads out and warms the surroundings a tiny bit. We say it is dissipated.

3-5.text: We can waste less energy. Oil on a bike chain cuts friction, so less energy is wasted heating the chain.

4-1.text: Part four. Efficiency. ... Efficiency tells you how much of the energy put in is useful. Efficiency equals useful energy out, divided by total energy in.

4-2.text: For the filament bulb: 20 joules divided by 100 joules is 0.2. As a percentage that is 20 percent. Only 20 percent of the energy is useful.

4-3.text: An electric motor is given 100 joules and 80 joules goes into its kinetic store. Its efficiency is 80 divided by 100, which is 80 percent.

4-4.text: LED bulbs waste much less energy heating the room than filament bulbs, so they are much more efficient.

4-5.text: No device can be more than 100 percent efficient. You can never get out more energy than you put in.

5-1.text: Part five. Energy resources. ... We need energy resources to make electricity, heat our homes and move cars, buses and planes.

5-2.text: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels. They formed from plants and animals over millions of years. They are non-renewable: one day they will run out.

5-3.text: Burning fossil fuels gives out carbon dioxide. This gas traps heat in the air, which adds to global warming.

5-4.text: Renewable resources will not run out: wind, solar (sunlight), hydroelectric (falling water), tides, waves and geothermal (heat from hot rocks underground).

5-5.text: But wind and solar depend on the weather. No wind, no spin. At night, no sunlight. Geothermal works in any weather.
